body: Monday, March 10 2025 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto
Information available before 2025-03-10 00:00 UTC. Prices use completed prior sessions. Prepared retrospectively; later outcomes are excluded.

Macro Stance: US growth is losing momentum while the Fed says it has no hurry. Powell told reporters there is no rush to move rates while trade policy stays unsettled [1], and Reuters reported he signalled possible changes to the dot-plot rate forecasts [2]. Hard data is softening at the margin. Payroll growth came in at 151,000 in February, less than expected [3]. ADP private payrolls showed the smallest gain since July, at 77,000 [4]. The latest services ISM print is 53.5 index points, a reading of an economy still growing rather than one overheating [5]. The risk is that federal layoffs and tariffs weigh on hiring through the spring, which is how the New York Times jobs coverage frames the report [6].

Rates & Curve: The 2Y yield is 3.99% and the 10Y is 4.32% at the prior close (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-07). The 10Y-2Y spread is 33 bps and the curve is positively sloped. Over 20 observations the 2Y has fallen 22 bps from 4.21% and the 10Y 13 bps from 4.45%, which is a bull steepening move with the 2Y down more. The spread has widened 9 bps over that window, and over five observations the 2Y is unchanged while the 10Y is up 8 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-07). The 3M sits at 4.34%, so the 10Y is 2 bps below the bill, and the 30Y-10Y spread is 30 bps. Equities are pricing the slowdown more than the bond market is. The S&P 500 closed at 5,770.20 after a 0.55% gain, but it is down 5.15% over 20 sessions and the VIX is at 23.37, up 50.77% over the same stretch (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The Russell 2000 at 2,075.48 has lost 10.04% over 20 sessions, a sharper drawdown than the large caps. The dollar index stands at 103.84 index points, down 3.58% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07).

New / Most Important: The signal that matters most is the mix of soft labour data and a tariff overhang, not a hot inflation print. Reuters previewed the week with the line that the US stock market faces an inflation data test [7], so the next hard print is still pending. Dollar weakness after the jobs report and Powell's comments [8] shows that currency markets are already pricing a slower path. Yahoo Finance argued that the 'Trump put' may be found in Treasurys rather than equities [9], and that is the right frame: investors are buying duration as the equity hedge. The administration is not offering a floor for stocks. Trump blamed globalists for the sell-off [10] and said tariffs could go up [11].

Playbook ✓: Stay underweight broad equity beta into the inflation print and the shutdown vote. The House vote Reuters reported as aimed at the coming Tuesday [12] and the warning that a shutdown is possible even if Trump expects it to be averted [13] are the two dated risks in the stack. Own duration (TLT, IEF) while the curve bull-steepens and the 20-session decline in the 2Y is intact; TLT is at 90.11 and IEF at 94.39 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Hedge the equity book with VIX calls, because volatility has already risen 50.77% over 20 sessions and the Nasdaq 100 is in correction [14]. What would change the call: a 2Y back above 4.21% would say the front end is repricing the no-hurry Fed rather than the growth scare, and a Nasdaq 100 close back above 21,774.07 (the level 20 sessions earlier) would show that the buyers' strike has ended [15].

Macro Stance: The euro area is trading the German fiscal turn. Berlin agreed to loosen the debt brake for defence and infrastructure [16], and the parties behind the deal are now negotiating a government [17]. Politico put the stakes plainly: Merz has two weeks to deliver the spending revolution [18]. Brussels added its own plan, which the Guardian reported as an €800bn effort to rearm Europe [19]. Markets read the package as a growth signal first. Euronews called it a 'whatever it takes' moment that sparked a rally [20], and the euro has climbed to 1.0788 against the dollar, up 3.87% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The DAX stands at 23,008.94, up 5.61% over 20 sessions, while the STOXX 600 is at 553.35 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07).

Credit & Inflation: Euro-area labour data is firm. Unemployment is 6.2%, with Italy falling but still among the highest [21]. The ECB cut its deposit-linked key rate to 2.5% [22] and said policy is becoming meaningfully less restrictive [23]. Italy's spread over Germany has dropped below 100 basis points [24], which is the periphery telling the same story as the core. The risk sits in the bund market. A bond selloff that began in Germany pushed borrowing costs up across the world [25], and fund managers are describing it as a once-in-a-generation move [26]. The euro's strength against the dollar has been a tailwind for European equities priced in dollars: Euro Stoxx 50 at 5,468.41 is up 2.69% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07), while the FEZ ETF has gained 8.00% over the same window.

New / Most Important: The most important EU signal is that the rerating has moved beyond defence. Eurostoxx and European indexes closed at records on the back of the spending pledge, with defence names leading [27]. The London market also hit a record as defence stocks rallied [28]. Investors are rotating out of US technology and into Europe [29], and the appetite for European assets is returning [30]. The clearest read-across is to German infrastructure: Geberit reported a sentiment boost from the German infrastructure fund [31], which points to construction and building-products demand rather than arms alone.

Playbook ✓: Own the European fiscal beneficiaries and keep the euro-denominated industrial exposure, but trim into spikes in bund yields rather than chasing the first leg. The autos are the exception: German carmakers are bracing for tariffs [32], and the sector deserves its own short. Watch for the coalition deal as the trigger that converts the spending plan into orders, and for a bund sell-off that spreads to equity duration as the signal to cut the leverage. The disagreement is about pace more than direction: even the optimists accept that defence orders take time, as Reuters reported arms makers warning that filling the Ukraine gap will take time [33].

Macro Stance: China is trying to buy growth with the budget while the price data and the trade data both point the other way. Consumer prices have dropped below zero for the first time in a year [34], which is the deflation problem Reuters said policy has so far only talked about: 'more words than deeds' on consumption [35]. The National People's Congress set the growth goal at around 5% [36] and the budget deficit at around 4% of GDP, a record [37]. Officials say there is room for more stimulus if growth slows [38], and economists told CNBC that a much stronger package is needed if the trade war intensifies [39]. The policy signal is clear. The question for the next two quarters is whether the spending reaches households and private demand, or stays in infrastructure and the state sector.

PMIs & Activity: The latest activity survey is the official non-manufacturing PMI, which was 50.4 in February [40], a reading just above the expansion line rather than a strong one. Trade is the weak leg. China's exports missed forecasts as US tariffs bit, and imports recorded their sharpest decline since July 2023 [41]. The Shanghai Composite closed at 3,372.55 index points, up 2.08% over 20 sessions, which says equity investors are reading the policy turn more generously than the activity data allows (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The national legislature opened its annual session with the message that the economy is stable [42], but the trade numbers and the deflation print are the evidence that will be read against it.

Credit Impulse: Credit impulse is being delivered through the budget more than through bank lending. The official budget deficit has been raised to its highest level in more than 30 years [43], and the finance minister has said China has more room to act on fiscal policy amid global uncertainties [44]. The widened fiscal window is the stated tool [45], and the state planner is setting up a national venture-capital guidance fund [46]. The banking-side signal is less encouraging. The developer Longfor's bonds sank deeper into junk territory [47], which tells you the property credit channel is still impaired. What would confirm the view is a monthly credit print in which household borrowing turns up while developer credit keeps shrinking, and until that appears the impulse is fiscal rather than private.

Property: Property is the sector that policy most wants to stabilise, and officials are claiming progress. A minister said the property sector is showing positive changes [48], and Global Times reported that the real-estate market keeps stabilising as policy support lifts confidence [49]. The concrete step under discussion is ending the price cap on local governments buying apartments, which Bloomberg reported Beijing is weighing [50]. The caution is that the stabilisation claim sits alongside the developer bond stress at Longfor [47] and luxury retailers closing more China outlets as spending shrinks [51]. Property is the place where the weak household balance sheet shows up most clearly, and it is the reason the consumer-price print matters more than any single activity survey.

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Fiscal policy is expanding on several fronts at once, and trade policy is pushing the other way. The defence budget is rising 7.2% [52], and business coverage says military spending is growing faster than the economy [53]. China is boosting food imports from Latin America and Europe to offset the US trade war [54], and it hit Canadian farm and food products with retaliatory tariffs [55] after hitting US agriculture [56]. Beijing also added 15 US companies to its export-control list [57]. On the supply side the state is cutting steel output to restructure the sector [58], which matters for commodity demand. The central bank continued buying gold, adding to reserves for a fourth straight month in February [59]. None of these measures is a demand-side stimulus on its own; they are the policy toolkit being set out in the same week.

Markets & Flows: Equity markets have moved well ahead of the macro numbers. The Hang Seng closed at 24,231.30, down 0.57% in the latest session but up 5.62% over five sessions and 14.66% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The China internet ETF KWEB is at 36.99 USD, up 16.28% over 20 sessions, and the CSI 300 ETF ASHR is at 27.03 USD, up 3.56% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Alibaba is the clearest single name: its ADR is at 140.62 USD, up 40.09% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07), after the company unveiled a reasoning model that sent the shares higher [60]. Hong Kong stocks capped their best week in two months on policy support [61]. The yuan is steady: USD/CNY is at 7.2506, down 0.51% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Goldman raised its emerging-market target on the AI-driven China rally [62].

New / Most Important: The signal that matters most is the gap between the equity rally and the price data. Consumer prices turned negative [34], the export and import numbers are weak [41], and the property signals are mixed [48][47]. Against that, the equity market has priced a policy put with real conviction, and the Alibaba move is a sentiment indicator as much as a fundamental one [63]. The retaliatory tariff exchanges with Canada and the US show that trade friction is spreading beyond Washington [64]. The new information in the set is that officials are now openly discussing more stimulus if growth slows [38], which is a policy reaction to the weak data rather than a sign that the data is already turning.

Playbook ✓: Hold China exposure through the internet and policy-sensitive names rather than the broad consumer or property complex. The trade is a fiscal-liquidity story with a deflation cap: buy the dips in the state-backed and platform names while the stimulus language keeps rising, and keep property exposure small until the developer credit channel stops shrinking. A move in USD/CNY back toward 7.29, the level 20 sessions earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-02-07), would signal that the policy easing is being offset by capital outflow, and the position should be cut. What would confirm the broader recovery is a property stabilisation that shows up in developer credit and an improvement in the export data. ⚠ Divergence: the Hang Seng is up 14.66% over 20 sessions while consumer prices have turned negative and exports missed forecasts, so the rally is pricing a policy outcome that the activity data has not yet delivered.

Macro Stance: Japan is moving toward the end of deflation, and the Bank of Japan's hike path is the dominant story. Inflation climbed to a two-year high of 4% in January [65], and the Japan Times said the reading keeps the BOJ on its hike path [66]. A government minister said Japan is ready to declare an end to deflation [67]. Labour is pushing the same way: the largest union group is asking for the biggest wage increase in more than 30 years [68]. Sources told Reuters that inflation risks could prompt a discussion of a rate hike in May [69]. Former BOJ governor Kuroda said Japan must fix the misunderstanding that it is manipulating the yen [70].

Activity & Currency: Japanese bonds have been the transmission channel. The 10-year yield hit its highest level in over 15 years [71], and traders placed a record bet on a stronger yen with more hikes in view [72]. The currency has responded: USD/JPY is at 148.1080, down 2.04% over 20 sessions and 0.53% in the latest session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The Nikkei 225 closed at 36,887.17, down 5.01% over 20 sessions and 2.17% in the prior session, a drawdown that is larger than the broader Japan ETF, which is up 1.11% over the same window (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Real activity is softer than the price story. Corporate capital spending fell for the first time in four years amid tariff fears [73], and the current account slipped into deficit for the first time in two years [74].

Playbook ✓: Favour domestic-demand names and the banks over the yen-sensitive exporters while USD/JPY trades under 151.19, the level 20 sessions earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The trade is a rates story with a currency kicker: a stronger yen compresses exporter earnings, so the exporters are the short leg and domestic wage beneficiaries the long leg. Watch the May discussion [69] as the pending trigger. A dovish tone there would cut the yen rally short and help the Nikkei recover its 20-session loss; a firmer tone would extend the move in JGB yields and push the yen toward the strong end of the range. Japan's exposure to US auto tariffs keeps the exporter short credible regardless of the currency path [75].

Macro Stance: Australia's economy grew faster in the final quarter, with GDP up 1.3% and exports doing the work [76]. The per-capita recession has ended, after 21 months [77], and Bloomberg read the acceleration as backing the RBA's hawkish tone [78]. That reading sits awkwardly with the market. The RBA made its latest rate cut in February [79], and Governor Bullock is weighing a series of global storms cautiously [80]. Economists are calling the recovery shallow [81], and the ABC is asking whether the economy has turned the corner at all [82]. The central bank's rate path is not the driver of the sell-off; the banks and the iron-ore chain are.

Demand & Financing: The Australian dollar is at 0.6332, up 0.80% over 20 sessions, while the S&P/ASX 200 closed at 7,948.20, down 1.81% in the latest session, 2.74% over five sessions and 6.62% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Commonwealth Bank has lost 8.71% over 20 sessions, closing at 148.50 AUD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07), and short sellers are ditching CBA as the sell-off doubts mount [83]. The AFR's view is that the ASX sell-off is getting serious and that banks and passive flows are to blame [84]. Iron ore is the second leg. China's cuts to steel output are piling pressure on Australian iron ore [85], and disruptions to shipments already hit China's January-February imports [86]. BHP sits at 38.98 AUD, down 3.71% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07).

Playbook ✓: Underweight the ASX banks into the next data print and the China steel signal. Commonwealth Bank is the cleanest expression: short on rallies toward the 162.67 AUD level from 20 sessions earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07), with the risk that dividend cuts across the market keep the sector bid lower [87]. Use the AUD as a yield and iron-ore proxy rather than a risk-on currency: it has held firm while equities fell, so the currency is not confirming the equity signal. The call changes if the ASX reclaims its 20-session reference of 8,511.40 or if iron-ore imports recover, which would show the Chinese steel cuts were a short-term supply move rather than a demand signal.

Macro Stance: Poland's economy is in a better place than the headlines about tariffs suggest. Eurostat put Poland at the lowest unemployment rate on record and joint-lowest in the EU [88], and a Polish-language survey read says the manufacturing PMI points to a recovery after almost three years of contraction [89]. GUS's latest GDP release shows the economy accelerating [90], while the January CPI edged higher [91]. The central bank is not in a hurry: one commentary argued inflation will rise further and that this is a strong argument for the RPP on rates [92]. Wages rose in 2024 [93], and Pekao expects household consumption to stay strong through 2025 [94]. The strong zloty is the one drag the forecasters flag: Santander warned it could weigh on GDP [95].

Markets: The zloty has been the strongest currency story in the region. USD/PLN is at 3.8671, down 4.14% over 20 sessions and 3.41% over five, and EUR/PLN is at 4.1715, down 0.43% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Bankier asked who is hurt by a strong zloty and noted that the currency has been this strong only once before in its history [96], while Strefa Inwestorów reported the euro at its cheapest since 2018 [97]. Equities are catching up with the currency. The WIG20 tracker is at 50.19 PLN, up 6.15% over 20 sessions, and the iShares Poland ETF EPOL is at 27.42 USD, up 13.31% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Parkiet headlined huge gains on the exchange and asked whether Europe is catching the wind in its sails [98], and its analysts say the strong zloty is supporting the WIG20 [99]. Foreign central banks are buying Polish government bonds, with more than 10 holding them [100] and the buyers described as big, strong players [101]. Benefit Systems placed five-year bonds with demand above 1.6bn zloty [102], a sign that credit appetite is intact.

Fiscal & Politics: The fiscal debate is about the deficit and the defence bill. Brussels is easing the excessive-deficit rules, and the open question is whether Poland gains or loses [103]. The government has promised a defence build-up [104], and the president has pledged to spend 4.7% of GDP on defence this year [105]. Reserve numbers are part of the plan, with the reserve force counted at more than 300 thousand people [106]. Politics is less settled. Prime Minister Tusk has already set a confidence vote for the government [107], and an opposition MP was detained over alleged financial crimes [108]. The fiscal story is therefore a political story as much as a budget one: the spending is popular, the deficit is the cost, and the vote is the test.

Corporate & Sectors: Energy and defence lead the corporate story, and the banks and consumer names are the ballast. Dino Polska's shares hit an all-time high [109], and PKO and Pekao have been part of the banking rally, with PKO up 8.18% over 20 sessions at 73.00 PLN (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Orlen is the largest move: the shares are at 64.46 PLN, up 14.82% over 20 sessions, after the group set a record for gas output [110] and signed a carbon-capture development with Equinor [111]. Orlen is also cooperating with Ukraine's Naftogaz on LNG [112]. KGHM is the laggard: its CEO said in his first interview that years of neglect left the company short of investment [113], and the shares are down 0.49% over 20 sessions. Index changes are the near-term mechanism. CCC and Zabka join the WIG20 after the session of 21 March, and Cyfrowy Polsat and JSW leave [114][115].

Geopolitics & Security: Security is now the policy driver. Poland will require every adult man to take military training [116], and it has asked NATO to raise the defence-spending floor to 3% of GDP [117]. The government is also seeking access to nuclear arms [118], and the premier said Poland must look at nuclear options, alarmed by Trump's direction [119]. The Macron proposal on a European nuclear umbrella was welcomed in Warsaw and the Baltics [120]. The Ukraine data point is the Starlink spat. Musk said Ukraine can keep Starlink [121], while Sikorski said Poland will seek alternatives if access is cut [122]. Poland is also buying more South Korean K2 tanks in a 6.2bn dollar deal [123], which is the procurement pipeline behind the defence equities.

New / Most Important: The signal that matters most is that the Warsaw market is now being led by a combination of the strong zloty, foreign bond buying and defence procurement. The Polish press has tied the defence boom to the stock index directly: defence shares are the hottest product on the market [124], and the military-stocks story is moving the WIG20 [125]. That makes the index more sensitive to a peace headline than it was a month ago, because a lower defence premium would hit the index's most dynamic names first. The second signal is that the market is pricing the zloty's strength as a sign of confidence, while the exporters carry the cost [95].

Playbook ✓: Own the Polish market through the banks and the energy and defence names, but keep the currency leg as the hedge rather than the bet. The trade is a yield-and-currency story with a defence kicker: buy the WIG20 tracker on dips while USD/PLN stays below the 4.03 level it held 20 sessions earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-02-07), and add to Orlen and the banks on the index rebalancing if the flows confirm it. Cut the position if the Ukraine talks turn into a peace framework, because the defence names carry the premium and would reprice first, and if the central bank's tone turns dovish while the zloty is still strong. ⚠ Divergence: the zloty is up sharply against the dollar and the WIG20 is up 6.15% over 20 sessions, but the same strength is the headwind that Santander flags for exporters and GDP, so the equity rally is running ahead of the growth signal.

Narrative: Technology is the consensus AI winner, yet the sector ETF is down 6.94% over 20 sessions and the semiconductor index is down 9.09% over the same stretch. XLK closed at 218.54 after a 1.45% gain in the latest session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Investors are rewarding AI demand and punishing the multiple at the same time, and the sector's direction depends on which signal wins. Microsoft's in-house models that it believes rival OpenAI's [126] keep the software-platform story alive.

Reported: Broadcom beat on AI revenue, which rose 77% in the quarter [127], and the Barron's read was that the AI trade is not dead [128]. Marvell had the opposite reaction: its shares ended their worst day in 24 years after a tepid revenue forecast [129]. Apple cut the price of its new MacBook Air [130], a volume move that does not change the sector's earnings path on its own.

EPS Upside Watch: The best upside candidates are the names with fresh demand evidence. Broadcom's forecast eased demand worries for AI chips [131], and the next set of estimate revisions is likely to move up for the AI-infrastructure names that guided higher. Marvell is the reverse case: its shares are down 40.59% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07), so the bar for a surprise is lower, but the guidance has to change first.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Nvidia led chipmakers lower on fears that AI demand is slowing [132], even as Broadcom's beat was read as proof the cycle is intact. Nvidia is down 12.43% over 20 sessions and closed at 112.69 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The convention that AI leadership is simple breaks here: a strong beat from one name does not protect the group when the leader is de-rating.

Narrative: Communication services has lagged on ad-cycle worries and regulatory risk. XLC is at 100.29, down 2.59% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07), while Netflix has fallen 12.26% and Meta 12.13% over the same window. The Justice Department's revised proposal still calls for Google to divest Chrome, though it allows AI investments [133], which keeps the platform overhang in the group's price.

Reported: Reddit's ad revenue is growing faster than other social platforms [134], which is the one clear positive in the set. Sphere Entertainment missed earnings forecasts in its fourth quarter, though it promised a stronger 2025 [135]. Those results are the mixed backdrop for the sector: pockets of growth and misses in the entertainment names.

EPS Upside Watch: The upside case rests on Alphabet's AI and autonomous-driving spend. Its CFO offered a bullish view of Waymo as the future of transportation [136], and Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses are being positioned as a successor to the smartphone [137]. Both are optionality rather than near-term EPS, so the upside watch is narrow and depends on guidance that has not yet been given.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says the platform giants are the safest AI spenders. The sector's own leaders are down 12% over 20 sessions in Meta and Netflix, which says the market is not paying for that safety. Investors are treating ad revenue and legal risk as the binding constraint, not AI capex.

Narrative: Financials are trading on the recession argument. The Wall Street Journal said the recession trade is back [138], and the stagflation risk is the one that bank stocks cannot price cleanly [139]. XLF closed at 49.12, down 5.74% over 20 sessions, and regional banks are down 11.92% over the same window, with KRE at 57.69 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Goldman Sachs is down 14.97% over 20 sessions.

Reported: Blackstone beat its full-year expectations [140] and Merchants Bancorp beat too [141], while Customers Bancorp missed on EPS [142]. The reported set is mixed, but the market is looking past it to the macro signal.

EPS Upside Watch: Banks may be gaining share in large financings. Private credit eased off mega loan deals as the banks regained ground [143], which would lift fee income if the trend holds. Hedge-fund fee pressure is the offset: Goldman's view is that hedge funds have given up half their 2025 gains in a challenging market [144], which weighs on prime-brokerage revenue.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency rescinded a key regulatory hurdle for banks engaging in crypto-related activity [145]. That is a structural positive for the banks' fee franchise, and it is being ignored by a sector that is trading purely on the macro. The convention that banks trade on rates breaks when the regulatory calendar shifts.

Narrative: Oil is being pulled between geopolitics and demand. WTI closed at 67.04, down 5.06% over 20 sessions, and Brent at 70.36, down 5.29% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Iran's leader rebuffed a letter calling for nuclear talks [146], and the US is weighing a plan to disrupt Iranian oil by halting vessels at sea [147]. OPEC's February output rose as Iranian exports kept flowing [148]. XLE closed at 87.43, up 1.71% in the latest session.

Reported: Energy earnings were soft. BP's chief executive faces a 30% pay cut after a profit miss and Elliott's intervention [149]. Harbour Energy's shares sank to a record low after a profit hit from the UK windfall tax [150], and Aramco expects a lower 2025 dividend after net income fell [151].

EPS Upside Watch: US natural gas is the upside. Henry Hub closed at 4.40 USD, up 29.08% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07), and producers are talking about a boom [152]. That favours the gas-weighted producers over the oil majors, which are more exposed to the lower crude price.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The convention that Iran risk means higher oil is breaking. Treasury's secretary said the US will collapse Iran's economy by shutting down its oil industry [153], a supply threat, yet crude is down over 20 sessions. The market is treating demand weakness as the bigger force, which is the opposite of the headline geopolitics.

Narrative: Industrials are caught between European capex and US tariff costs. The dominant popular-narrative trade is Germany's rearmament, which is treated like a picks-and-shovels capex wave and which moves with the mechanics of the GameStop effect that Reuters tied to Eutelsat's 650% surge [263], the same reflexive pattern that drives any buildout-led speculative run.

Why Retail Is Here: The story the crowd tells itself is simple. Germany has agreed a bumper spending package and moved to lift its debt brake [264], and the EU has put an €800bn rearmament plan on the table [19]. That reads as a multi-year order book for the arms makers, the kind of thing that cannot be cut by the next election. The emotional hook is 'whatever it takes', and the old frugal Germany is back [20][265]. Rheinmetall, at 1,115.00 EUR, is the name the trade uses as its proxy, and the 723.40 EUR level from twenty sessions earlier and the round 1,000 EUR figure are the levels that make a dip look like a gift.

What Is Driving It: The hard numbers are the strongest part of the story. Rheinmetall closed at 1,115.00 EUR, up 54.13% over 20 sessions from 723.40 EUR, up 10.78% over five sessions, and down 7.01% in the latest session, which is the kind of sharp drawdown dip-buyers typically buy (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Siemens is up 12.94% over 20 sessions at 234.30 EUR (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The cross-asset backdrop is European: the DAX is up 5.61% over 20 sessions and the euro is up 3.87% against the dollar (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07), while the US aerospace-and-defence ETF is down 4.64% over the same window. European defence led the record closes on the pledge [27], and Euronews called the fiscal boost the spark for a market rally [20]. The divergence with the US defence ETF is the tell: the price is paying for a European story, not for the sector.

The Social Signal: The clearest signal is the Reuters line that retail traders were behind Eutelsat's 650% surge, which it called the GameStop effect [263]. Eutelsat tripled on the EU defence-spending plan [266] and then slipped as investors paused the rally on Ukraine prospects [248], which is what a crowd chasing a headline looks like on a chart. The Polish retail press is louder still: Bankier wrote that the defence industry is the hottest commodity on the market, with shares setting new records [124], and Investing.com Polska named Rheinmetall, Hensoldt and Renk as the German names rising sharply [267]. Bankier also headlined a military battalion on the exchange, with listed companies earning from the military boom [125].

Historical Analog: The mechanical analogy is the GameStop squeeze, which Reuters named in its piece on Eutelsat [263]. The first wave is a real repricing: a credible policy change moves the cash flows of a set of companies, and the shares re-rate on the news. The second wave is retail, which arrives once the first move is visible on a chart and the story is repeated enough times to feel like a sure thing. What makes it dangerous is that the second wave buys the second derivative of the news, the expected order book, rather than the orders themselves, so the first disappointment on delivery hits the most crowded names first.

Smart Money View: Institutions support the trade, but they disagree about pace. The Wall Street Journal reported that overlooked European defence stocks became a hedge-fund home run [268], and Citi says Lockheed and five other defence stocks look like buys after a slump [269]. The Economist's line is that as Germany's defence stocks go ballistic, the arms makers are tooling up [270]. The sceptics argue the spending will not fix the economy: a Guardian commentary argues military spending is no remedy for Britain's ailing economy [271], and Reuters reported that arms makers say filling the Ukraine gap will take time [33]. Morningstar's fund managers are reacting to the bund selloff at the same time [26]. The disagreement is about pace, not direction: the spending itself is on the record, but the sceptics think the orders arrive later than the price assumes.

When the Narrative Breaks: The first observable break is the round number: a daily close back under 1,000 EUR would signal the 1,115.00 EUR level has failed, and the 723.40 EUR reference is the line that would show the entire 20-session move has been erased. The second trigger is a peace track. US-Ukraine talks are planned in Saudi Arabia [249], and Merz has two weeks to deliver the spending revolution [18]; a framework that calms the front would deflate the premium first. The third is the bund: the bond selloff that began in Germany pushed borrowing costs up around the world [25], and a sustained rise in German yields hits the long-duration defence names through their valuations. The instrument risk is liquidity: a euro-listed single stock with a retail crowd can gap on a single headline, and the US ETF divergence (down 4.64% over 20 sessions) shows the trade is not a sector-wide bid.

Why Retail Is Here: The pitch is that the state has finally joined the bitcoin trade. Trump signed the executive order establishing a strategic bitcoin reserve [272], which adds 200,000 seized bitcoins, per Fortune [219]. The hook is that a government stockpile is a floor under the price, a 'digital Fort Knox', as Yahoo Finance put it [273]. CNN's explainer for newcomers [274] and the White House crypto czar's line that the public has lost out on over $17 billion in bitcoin value [275] are the material that draws newcomers.

Where It Breaks: The price evidence is the reverse of the story. CNBC reported on 6 March that bitcoin fell even after Trump officially established the reserve [218]. Bitcoin closed at 80,601.04 USD, down 6.45% in the latest session and 15.84% over 20 sessions from 95,773.38 (Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2025-03-09), while ether is down 26.53% and Solana 28.84% over the same window. A close back above 95,773.38 would say the reserve headline finally works; a close under 80,601.04 would confirm the floor has gone. The instrument risk is the proxy chain: the iShares bitcoin ETF is down 10.32% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). A pending bill that the crypto summit called for before August [276] is the policy event to watch.

Why Retail Is Here: The pitch is a clean comeback. Western Digital has left the SSD market and SanDisk takes over the flash operations [277], and Wccftech puts it more bluntly: SanDisk will now be responsible for existing and future products [278]. Stocktwits headlined an analyst's prediction of nearly 70% upside for the relisted stock, and said retail is excited [279]. The product news keeps the brand in front of buyers: Forbes reports that SanDisk unveiled a fast USB4 portable SSD [280], and a review of the SanDisk Fortnite Peely Edition drive ran on 8 March [281]. The hook is a memory name that is newly listed and already has a consumer brand behind it.

Where It Breaks: SanDisk closed at 51.00 USD on 7 March, up 9.68% in the latest session and 8.86% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The first trigger is the 51.00 close, because any close below it means part of the latest session's surge is already gone. The instrument risk is the newness. The handover was reported only on 6 March [277], so the listed company has a short record of its own, and a share with that history can gap on one headline in either direction.

Why Retail Is Here: The pitch is that the boycott has made the stock cheap. Yahoo Finance headlined a 45% fall from the record high as a 'gut check moment' that has Wall Street bulls doubling down [282], and CNBC reports that the shares have declined every week since Elon Musk went to Washington [283]. The weekly losses read as a discount rather than a verdict on the cars. The used market points the same way: Forbes headlines a used-car price crash, with Model Y and Model 3 deals exploding [284]. The pitch is simple: the political damage is temporary, and both the car and the stock are on sale while it lasts.

Where It Breaks: Tesla closed at 262.67 USD, down 0.30% in the latest session, 10.35% over five sessions and 29.83% over 20 from 374.32 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). A rebound would have to reclaim the 374.32 reference to prove the bargain call, and a daily close below 262.67 would extend the five-session slide. Fortune reports that Tesla is flailing in China as BYD rises [285], and Reuters reports dozens protesting at a Tesla showroom in Portugal ahead of a likely snap election [286]. The instrument risk is that options amplify a move in either direction.

geo.label: hold / growth-scare watch
parts: Macro Stance

US growth is losing momentum while the Fed says it has no hurry. Powell told reporters there is no rush to move rates while trade policy stays unsettled [[n11891]], and Reuters reported he signalled possible changes to the dot-plot rate forecasts [[n11869]]. Hard data is softening at the margin. Payroll growth came in at 151,000 in February, less than expected [[n11453]]. ADP private payrolls showed the smallest gain since July, at 77,000 [[n11216]]. The latest services ISM print is 53.5 index points, a reading of an economy still growing rather than one overheating [[n11197]]. The risk is that federal layoffs and tariffs weigh on hiring through the spring, which is how the New York Times jobs coverage frames the report [[n11403]].
Rates & Curve

The 2Y yield is 3.99% and the 10Y is 4.32% at the prior close (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-07). The 10Y-2Y spread is 33 bps and the curve is positively sloped. Over 20 observations the 2Y has fallen 22 bps from 4.21% and the 10Y 13 bps from 4.45%, which is a bull steepening move with the 2Y down more. The spread has widened 9 bps over that window, and over five observations the 2Y is unchanged while the 10Y is up 8 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-07). The 3M sits at 4.34%, so the 10Y is 2 bps below the bill, and the 30Y-10Y spread is 30 bps. Equities are pricing the slowdown more than the bond market is. The S&P 500 closed at 5,770.20 after a 0.55% gain, but it is down 5.15% over 20 sessions and the VIX is at 23.37, up 50.77% over the same stretch (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The Russell 2000 at 2,075.48 has lost 10.04% over 20 sessions, a sharper drawdown than the large caps. The dollar index stands at 103.84 index points, down 3.58% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07).
New / Most Important

The signal that matters most is the mix of soft labour data and a tariff overhang, not a hot inflation print. Reuters previewed the week with the line that the US stock market faces an inflation data test [[n0520]], so the next hard print is still pending. Dollar weakness after the jobs report and Powell's comments [[n4201]] shows that currency markets are already pricing a slower path. Yahoo Finance argued that the 'Trump put' may be found in Treasurys rather than equities [[n11899]], and that is the right frame: investors are buying duration as the equity hedge. The administration is not offering a floor for stocks. Trump blamed globalists for the sell-off [[n11838]] and said tariffs could go up [[n11920]].
Playbook ✓

Stay underweight broad equity beta into the inflation print and the shutdown vote. The House vote Reuters reported as aimed at the coming Tuesday [[n11842]] and the warning that a shutdown is possible even if Trump expects it to be averted [[n11921]] are the two dated risks in the stack. Own duration (TLT, IEF) while the curve bull-steepens and the 20-session decline in the 2Y is intact; TLT is at 90.11 and IEF at 94.39 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Hedge the equity book with VIX calls, because volatility has already risen 50.77% over 20 sessions and the Nasdaq 100 is in correction [[n11874]]. What would change the call: a 2Y back above 4.21% would say the front end is repricing the no-hurry Fed rather than the growth scare, and a Nasdaq 100 close back above 21,774.07 (the level 20 sessions earlier) would show that the buyers' strike has ended [[n11878]].

geo.label: fiscal pivot, easing bias
parts: Macro Stance

The euro area is trading the German fiscal turn. Berlin agreed to loosen the debt brake for defence and infrastructure [[n3540]], and the parties behind the deal are now negotiating a government [[n3706]]. Politico put the stakes plainly: Merz has two weeks to deliver the spending revolution [[n3679]]. Brussels added its own plan, which the Guardian reported as an €800bn effort to rearm Europe [[n3459]]. Markets read the package as a growth signal first. Euronews called it a 'whatever it takes' moment that sparked a rally [[n3680]], and the euro has climbed to 1.0788 against the dollar, up 3.87% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The DAX stands at 23,008.94, up 5.61% over 20 sessions, while the STOXX 600 is at 553.35 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07).
Credit & Inflation

Euro-area labour data is firm. Unemployment is 6.2%, with Italy falling but still among the highest [[n11039]]. The ECB cut its deposit-linked key rate to 2.5% [[n3606]] and said policy is becoming meaningfully less restrictive [[n3611]]. Italy's spread over Germany has dropped below 100 basis points [[n3534]], which is the periphery telling the same story as the core. The risk sits in the bund market. A bond selloff that began in Germany pushed borrowing costs up across the world [[n3594]], and fund managers are describing it as a once-in-a-generation move [[n3684]]. The euro's strength against the dollar has been a tailwind for European equities priced in dollars: Euro Stoxx 50 at 5,468.41 is up 2.69% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07), while the FEZ ETF has gained 8.00% over the same window.
New / Most Important

The most important EU signal is that the rerating has moved beyond defence. Eurostoxx and European indexes closed at records on the back of the spending pledge, with defence names leading [[n3407]]. The London market also hit a record as defence stocks rallied [[n7050]]. Investors are rotating out of US technology and into Europe [[n3530]], and the appetite for European assets is returning [[n3560]]. The clearest read-across is to German infrastructure: Geberit reported a sentiment boost from the German infrastructure fund [[n3640]], which points to construction and building-products demand rather than arms alone.
Playbook ✓

Own the European fiscal beneficiaries and keep the euro-denominated industrial exposure, but trim into spikes in bund yields rather than chasing the first leg. The autos are the exception: German carmakers are bracing for tariffs [[n3685]], and the sector deserves its own short. Watch for the coalition deal as the trigger that converts the spending plan into orders, and for a bund sell-off that spreads to equity duration as the signal to cut the leverage. The disagreement is about pace more than direction: even the optimists accept that defence orders take time, as Reuters reported arms makers warning that filling the Ukraine gap will take time [[n7752]].

geo.label: stimulus-led, data still soft
parts: Macro Stance

China is trying to buy growth with the budget while the price data and the trade data both point the other way. Consumer prices have dropped below zero for the first time in a year [[n1602]], which is the deflation problem Reuters said policy has so far only talked about: 'more words than deeds' on consumption [[n1322]]. The National People's Congress set the growth goal at around 5% [[n1264]] and the budget deficit at around 4% of GDP, a record [[n1263]]. Officials say there is room for more stimulus if growth slows [[n1435]], and economists told CNBC that a much stronger package is needed if the trade war intensifies [[n1429]]. The policy signal is clear. The question for the next two quarters is whether the spending reaches households and private demand, or stays in infrastructure and the state sector.
PMIs & Activity

The latest activity survey is the official non-manufacturing PMI, which was 50.4 in February [[n0937]], a reading just above the expansion line rather than a strong one. Trade is the weak leg. China's exports missed forecasts as US tariffs bit, and imports recorded their sharpest decline since July 2023 [[n1422]]. The Shanghai Composite closed at 3,372.55 index points, up 2.08% over 20 sessions, which says equity investors are reading the policy turn more generously than the activity data allows (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The national legislature opened its annual session with the message that the economy is stable [[n1285]], but the trade numbers and the deflation print are the evidence that will be read against it.
Credit Impulse

Credit impulse is being delivered through the budget more than through bank lending. The official budget deficit has been raised to its highest level in more than 30 years [[n1246]], and the finance minister has said China has more room to act on fiscal policy amid global uncertainties [[n1415]]. The widened fiscal window is the stated tool [[n1273]], and the state planner is setting up a national venture-capital guidance fund [[n1419]]. The banking-side signal is less encouraging. The developer Longfor's bonds sank deeper into junk territory [[n1292]], which tells you the property credit channel is still impaired. What would confirm the view is a monthly credit print in which household borrowing turns up while developer credit keeps shrinking, and until that appears the impulse is fiscal rather than private.
Property

Property is the sector that policy most wants to stabilise, and officials are claiming progress. A minister said the property sector is showing positive changes [[n1601]], and Global Times reported that the real-estate market keeps stabilising as policy support lifts confidence [[n1604]]. The concrete step under discussion is ending the price cap on local governments buying apartments, which Bloomberg reported Beijing is weighing [[n1417]]. The caution is that the stabilisation claim sits alongside the developer bond stress at Longfor [[n1292]] and luxury retailers closing more China outlets as spending shrinks [[n1611]]. Property is the place where the weak household balance sheet shows up most clearly, and it is the reason the consumer-price print matters more than any single activity survey.
Fiscal, Policy & Trade

Fiscal policy is expanding on several fronts at once, and trade policy is pushing the other way. The defence budget is rising 7.2% [[n6142]], and business coverage says military spending is growing faster than the economy [[n6143]]. China is boosting food imports from Latin America and Europe to offset the US trade war [[n1270]], and it hit Canadian farm and food products with retaliatory tariffs [[n1514]] after hitting US agriculture [[n1094]]. Beijing also added 15 US companies to its export-control list [[n1089]]. On the supply side the state is cutting steel output to restructure the sector [[n1092]], which matters for commodity demand. The central bank continued buying gold, adding to reserves for a fourth straight month in February [[n1519]]. None of these measures is a demand-side stimulus on its own; they are the policy toolkit being set out in the same week.
Markets & Flows

Equity markets have moved well ahead of the macro numbers. The Hang Seng closed at 24,231.30, down 0.57% in the latest session but up 5.62% over five sessions and 14.66% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The China internet ETF KWEB is at 36.99 USD, up 16.28% over 20 sessions, and the CSI 300 ETF ASHR is at 27.03 USD, up 3.56% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Alibaba is the clearest single name: its ADR is at 140.62 USD, up 40.09% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07), after the company unveiled a reasoning model that sent the shares higher [[n1390]]. Hong Kong stocks capped their best week in two months on policy support [[n1535]]. The yuan is steady: USD/CNY is at 7.2506, down 0.51% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Goldman raised its emerging-market target on the AI-driven China rally [[n4104]].
New / Most Important

The signal that matters most is the gap between the equity rally and the price data. Consumer prices turned negative [[n1602]], the export and import numbers are weak [[n1422]], and the property signals are mixed [[n1601]][[n1292]]. Against that, the equity market has priced a policy put with real conviction, and the Alibaba move is a sentiment indicator as much as a fundamental one [[n1500]]. The retaliatory tariff exchanges with Canada and the US show that trade friction is spreading beyond Washington [[n1576]]. The new information in the set is that officials are now openly discussing more stimulus if growth slows [[n1435]], which is a policy reaction to the weak data rather than a sign that the data is already turning.
Playbook ✓

Hold China exposure through the internet and policy-sensitive names rather than the broad consumer or property complex. The trade is a fiscal-liquidity story with a deflation cap: buy the dips in the state-backed and platform names while the stimulus language keeps rising, and keep property exposure small until the developer credit channel stops shrinking. A move in USD/CNY back toward 7.29, the level 20 sessions earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-02-07), would signal that the policy easing is being offset by capital outflow, and the position should be cut. What would confirm the broader recovery is a property stabilisation that shows up in developer credit and an improvement in the export data. ⚠ Divergence: the Hang Seng is up 14.66% over 20 sessions while consumer prices have turned negative and exports missed forecasts, so the rally is pricing a policy outcome that the activity data has not yet delivered.

geo.label: hike path, strong yen
parts: Macro Stance

Japan is moving toward the end of deflation, and the Bank of Japan's hike path is the dominant story. Inflation climbed to a two-year high of 4% in January [[n5397]], and the Japan Times said the reading keeps the BOJ on its hike path [[n5408]]. A government minister said Japan is ready to declare an end to deflation [[n5583]]. Labour is pushing the same way: the largest union group is asking for the biggest wage increase in more than 30 years [[n5584]]. Sources told Reuters that inflation risks could prompt a discussion of a rate hike in May [[n5581]]. Former BOJ governor Kuroda said Japan must fix the misunderstanding that it is manipulating the yen [[n5608]].
Activity & Currency

Japanese bonds have been the transmission channel. The 10-year yield hit its highest level in over 15 years [[n5548]], and traders placed a record bet on a stronger yen with more hikes in view [[n5503]]. The currency has responded: USD/JPY is at 148.1080, down 2.04% over 20 sessions and 0.53% in the latest session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The Nikkei 225 closed at 36,887.17, down 5.01% over 20 sessions and 2.17% in the prior session, a drawdown that is larger than the broader Japan ETF, which is up 1.11% over the same window (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Real activity is softer than the price story. Corporate capital spending fell for the first time in four years amid tariff fears [[n5483]], and the current account slipped into deficit for the first time in two years [[n11487]].
Playbook ✓

Favour domestic-demand names and the banks over the yen-sensitive exporters while USD/JPY trades under 151.19, the level 20 sessions earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). The trade is a rates story with a currency kicker: a stronger yen compresses exporter earnings, so the exporters are the short leg and domestic wage beneficiaries the long leg. Watch the May discussion [[n5581]] as the pending trigger. A dovish tone there would cut the yen rally short and help the Nikkei recover its 20-session loss; a firmer tone would extend the move in JGB yields and push the yen toward the strong end of the range. The per-capita recession has ended, after 21 months [[n0236]], and Bloomberg read the acceleration as backing the RBA's hawkish tone [[n0240]]. That reading sits awkwardly with the market. Economists are calling the recovery shallow [[n0307]], and the ABC is asking whether the economy has turned the corner at all [[n0460]]. The Australian dollar is at 0.6332, up 0.80% over 20 sessions, while the S&P/ASX 200 closed at 7,948.20, down 1.81% in the latest session, 2.74% over five sessions and 6.62% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Underweight the ASX banks into the next data print and the China steel signal. Commonwealth Bank is the cleanest expression: short on rallies toward the 162.67 AUD level from 20 sessions earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07), with the risk that dividend cuts across the market keep the sector bid lower [[n0229]]. Use the AUD as a yield and iron-ore proxy rather than a risk-on currency: it has held firm while equities fell, so the currency is not confirming the equity signal. The call changes if the ASX reclaims its 20-session reference of 8,511.40 or if iron-ore imports recover, which would show the Chinese steel cuts were a short-term supply move rather than a demand signal.

parts: Macro Stance

Poland's economy is in a better place than the headlines about tariffs suggest. Eurostat put Poland at the lowest unemployment rate on record and joint-lowest in the EU [[n5727]], and a Polish-language survey read says the manufacturing PMI points to a recovery after almost three years of contraction [[n6045]]. GUS's latest GDP release shows the economy accelerating [[n5845]], while the January CPI edged higher [[n5853]]. The central bank is not in a hurry: one commentary argued inflation will rise further and that this is a strong argument for the RPP on rates [[n5855]]. Wages rose in 2024 [[n6049]], and Pekao expects household consumption to stay strong through 2025 [[n6136]]. The strong zloty is the one drag the forecasters flag: Santander warned it could weigh on GDP [[n5964]].
Markets

The zloty has been the strongest currency story in the region. USD/PLN is at 3.8671, down 4.14% over 20 sessions and 3.41% over five, and EUR/PLN is at 4.1715, down 0.43% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Bankier asked who is hurt by a strong zloty and noted that the currency has been this strong only once before in its history [[n6291]], while Strefa Inwestorów reported the euro at its cheapest since 2018 [[n6004]]. Equities are catching up with the currency. The WIG20 tracker is at 50.19 PLN, up 6.15% over 20 sessions, and the iShares Poland ETF EPOL is at 27.42 USD, up 13.31% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Parkiet headlined huge gains on the exchange and asked whether Europe is catching the wind in its sails [[n6177]], and its analysts say the strong zloty is supporting the WIG20 [[n6182]]. Foreign central banks are buying Polish government bonds, with more than 10 holding them [[n6033]] and the buyers described as big, strong players [[n6048]]. Benefit Systems placed five-year bonds with demand above 1.6bn zloty [[n6065]], a sign that credit appetite is intact.
Fiscal & Politics

The fiscal debate is about the deficit and the defence bill. Brussels is easing the excessive-deficit rules, and the open question is whether Poland gains or loses [[n6212]]. The government has promised a defence build-up [[n6181]], and the president has pledged to spend 4.7% of GDP on defence this year [[n5639]]. Reserve numbers are part of the plan, with the reserve force counted at more than 300 thousand people [[n6223]]. Politics is less settled. Prime Minister Tusk has already set a confidence vote for the government [[n5731]], and an opposition MP was detained over alleged financial crimes [[n5755]]. The fiscal story is therefore a political story as much as a budget one: the spending is popular, the deficit is the cost, and the vote is the test.
Corporate & Sectors

Energy and defence lead the corporate story, and the banks and consumer names are the ballast. Dino Polska's shares hit an all-time high [[n6278]], and PKO and Pekao have been part of the banking rally, with PKO up 8.18% over 20 sessions at 73.00 PLN (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-07). Orlen is the largest move: the shares are at 64.46 PLN, up 14.82% over 20 sessions, after the group set a record for gas output [[n6236]] and signed a carbon-capture development with Equinor [[n6023]]. Orlen is also cooperating with Ukraine's Naftogaz on LNG [[n5764]]. KGHM is the laggard: its CEO said in his first interview that years of neglect left the company short of investment [[n6323]], and the shares are down 0.49% over 20 sessions. Index changes are the near-term mechanism. CCC and Zabka join the WIG20 after the session of 21 March, and Cyfrowy Polsat and JSW leave [[n6213]][[n6256]].
Geopolitics & Security

Security is now the policy driver. Poland will require every adult man to take military training [[n5754]], and it has asked NATO to raise the defence-spending floor to 3% of GDP [[n5751]]. The government is also seeking access to nuclear arms [[n5752]], and the premier said Poland must look at nuclear options, alarmed by Trump's direction [[n5738]]. The Macron proposal on a European nuclear umbrella was welcomed in Warsaw and the Baltics [[n5732]]. The Ukraine data point is the Starlink spat. Musk said Ukraine can keep Starlink [[n5771]], while Sikorski said Poland will seek alternatives if access is cut [[n5777]]. Poland is also buying more South Korean K2 tanks in a 6.2bn dollar deal [[n5774]], which is the procurement pipeline behind the defence equities.
New / Most Important

The signal that matters most is that the Warsaw market is now being led by a combination of the strong zloty, foreign bond buying and defence procurement. The Polish press has tied the defence boom to the stock index directly: defence shares are the hottest product on the market [[n6050]], and the military-stocks story is moving the WIG20 [[n6295]]. That makes the index more sensitive to a peace headline than it was a month ago, because a lower defence premium would hit the index's most dynamic names first. The second signal is that the market is pricing the zloty's strength as a sign of confidence, while the exporters carry the cost [[n5964]].
Playbook ✓

Own the Polish market through the banks and the energy and defence names, but keep the currency leg as the hedge rather than the bet. The trade is a yield-and-currency story with a defence kicker: buy the WIG20 tracker on dips while USD/PLN stays below the 4.03 level it held 20 sessions earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-02-07), and add to Orlen and the banks on the index rebalancing if the flows confirm it. Cut the position if the Ukraine talks turn into a peace framework, because the defence names carry the premium and would reprice first, and if the central bank's tone turns dovish while the zloty is still strong. ⚠ Divergence: the zloty is up sharply against the dollar and the WIG20 is up 6.15% over 20 sessions, but the same strength is the headwind that Santander flags for exporters and GDP, so the equity rally is running ahead of the growth signal.
